title: SLO Safe Mode: Emergency Capacity Escape Hatch and Evidence Workflow
author: Maya Chen
body:
Summary:
This runbook describes the ‘SLO Safe Mode’ — a guarded, automated and manual escape hatch used by SREs to preserve user-facing SLOs during large-scale capacity pressure or rapid error-budget burns. It defines triggers, staged remediation actions (traffic remapping, graceful degradation, model fallbacks), evidence collection requirements for incident review, and guidance for safe reversion.

Scope:
- Applies to production inference-facing services managed by the inference runtime (hosted and dedicated).
- Intended for incidents where SLOs (latency or availability) are at immediate risk due to sudden capacity loss, cascading failures, or extreme burst traffic.
- Not intended for single-tenant feature bugs or routine autoscaling events.

Definitions:
- SLOs referenced: Availability (successful request ratio per 30d window), Latency P95/P99 per route, Error budget = 1 - SLO.
- Burn rate: current error budget consumption rate relative to baseline (1x).
- Safe Mode: a set of progressively stronger mitigations intended to restore SLOs quickly while minimizing customer impact.

Preconditions (what must be in place before triggering Safe Mode):
1. On-call SRE and service owner are paged and acknowledged.
2. Runbook access (runbook editor, ops console) and rollback credentials available to responders.
3. Telemetry validity checks (prometheus, traces, request logs) configured and passing sanity tests (see Telemetry Checklist).
4. Fallback model binaries and prebuilt quantized variants are available in the model cache with signed manifests.

Automated Triggers (these should auto-open an incident and can optionally take stage-1 actions if enabled):
- Sustained error-budget burn rate > 3x for 10 minutes across any SLO partition affecting >10% of global traffic.
- P99 latency degradation > 2x baseline for 5 minutes accompanied by 5xx rate > 0.5%.
- Headroom < 15% across cluster capacity for > 2 minutes and autoscaler failing to add capacity.

Manual Triggers:
- Any engineer or product owner who observes customer-facing degradation may initiate Safe Mode via the incident console with an explanation and expected duration.

Safe Mode Stages and Actions (ordered weakest -> strongest):
Stage 0 – Observe (no automatic changes)
- Actions: create incident, tag traffic, run evidence capture (see Evidence Collection).
- Responsible: on-call SRE.

Stage 1 – Traffic Shaping & Prioritization (low-risk)
- Actions (ordered):
  - Apply token-priority admission controller to cap new non-priority requests to 60% of baseline ingress.
  - Enable lightweight request-level caching for repeated prefix queries (30s TTL).
  - Route high-cost model variants to dedicated pool where available.
- CLI examples:
  - curl -X POST https://ops.redwood/api/traffic-shaper -d '{"service":"inference","profile":"priority-first","limit_pct":60}'
  - kubectl annotate svc inference-frontend ops-safe-mode=stage1 --overwrite
- Expected impact: small increase in tail latency for low-priority requests; preserves SLOs for critical traffic.

Stage 2 – Graceful Degradation (medium-risk)
- Actions:
  - Disable non-essential features (e.g., long-context summarization, speculative rollouts) via feature-flag toggles.
  - Force model quantized fallback for non-PII routes: switch to q4_0 variants in model router.
  - Reduce max tokens and sampling temperature for free-tier requests by 25%.
- CLI examples:
  - redwoodctl feature-flag set --service inference --flag long_context --value false
  - redwoodctl model-router set-fallback --service inference --from=thebigmodel-v2 --to=thebigmodel-v2-q4
- Expected impact: measurable quality reduction in some requests; large reduction in per-token GPU time.

Stage 3 – Aggressive Capacity Rebalancing (high-risk)
- Actions:
  - Evict or throttle lower-tier tenants according to priority ledger (see Capacity Escrow policy).
  - Shift traffic regionally: route 25–50% of affected traffic to compatible alternative region with verified model parity.
  - Pause scheduled batch jobs and maintenance windows; reclaim reserved capacity.
- CLI examples:
  - opsctl tenant throttle --tenant-id t-123 --target-pct 20
  - opsctl route move --from region-us-east-1 --to region-us-west-2 --pct 30
- Expected impact: significant customer-visible throttling for low-tier tenants; restores SLO headroom quickly.

Stage 4 – Emergency Fallback (last resort)
- Actions:
  - Global activation of emergency model variant (small quantized binary) for all non-enterprise traffic.
  - Temporary global rate limit (hard cap) at configured emergency RPS.
  - If capacity loss is due to a hardware outage, deploy pre-provisioned reserve nodes (private pool) and shift stateful caches to cold store.
- CLI examples:
  - redwoodctl model-router emergency-activate --variant emergency-small-v1
  - opsctl cluster claim-reserves --pool emergency-reserve-1 --replicas 12
- Expected impact: degraded semantic quality and shorter outputs; SLOs restored for highest-priority traffic.

Telemetry Checklist (must be captured at trigger time and periodically during incident):
- Prometheus queries to record immediately (copy into incident evidence):
  - error_rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference",status=~"5.."}[1m])) by (route)
  - p99_latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference"}[5m])) by (le,route))
  - capacity_headroom: avg(node_available_gpu_percent) by (cluster)
- Traces: capture representative traces for 5 slow requests and 5 failed requests. Attach trace IDs to incident.
- Logs: collect first 5xx per minute samples for 30 minutes, include stack and model router decision logs.
- Model metrics: KV cache hit rate, KV cache evictions, per-model token throughput.

Evidence Collection and Incident Review Standards (minimum required):
1. Precise timeline with UTC timestamps for every action (automated trigger, manual escalation, each Safe Mode stage toggle).
2. Prometheus dashboard snapshot (+ raw PromQL queries used).
3. Representative traces and sample logs compressed and attached.
4. A short causal hypothesis and a minimal reproduce recipe (if feasible).
5. List of mitigations attempted with timestamps and outcomes (success/failure/partial).
6. Estimated customer impact (users affected, error vs latency, revenue/contract exposure).
7. SLO burn-rate graph for the 72 hours before the incident and 24 hours after reversion.

Rollback Criteria and Reversion Procedure:
- Stability window: all primary SLOs within 1.05x of baseline for 30 minutes with error budget burn rate < 0.5x.
- Rollback steps (reverse order of applied actions):
  1. Re-enable paused features and lift hard rate limits (Stage 4->3->2->1).
  2. Shift traffic back regionally in 10% increments with 10-minute observation windows.
  3. Rebuild KV caches progressively to avoid cache stampedes (stagger warm-ups).
- If rollback triggers SLO regression, immediately re-enter the previous Safe Mode stage and escalate for deep forensics.

Ownership, Communication, and Escalation:
- Primary owner: inference-runtime on-call SRE.
- Secondary owner: capacity & autoscale team.
- Leadership escalation: if Safe Mode remains > 60 minutes or Stage 3+ persists > 15 minutes, notify VP of SRE and Product.
- Customer comms: Customer Success drafts initial outbound if incident meets SLA thresholds; notify enterprise customers within 30 minutes for any Stage 3+.

Testing and Runbook Drills:
- Quarterly Safe Mode drills: simulate Stage 1 and Stage 3 scenarios in a synthetic traffic lab. Verify trigger thresholds and rollback sequence.
- Runbook rehearsal checklist:
  - Confirm simulated model fallback works and degraded outputs are acceptable to QA team.
  - Validate telemetry collection end-to-end (prom, traces, logs) and attachment automation.
  - Measure time-to-SLO-recovery for each stage target:
    - Stage 1 target: recover within 10 minutes.
    - Stage 3 target: recover within 30 minutes.

Operational Tooling Recipes (scripts, dashboards, automation hooks):
- Prometheus alert rule snippet (example):
  - alert: SLOBurnHigh
    expr: (sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference",status=~"5.."}[10m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference"}[10m]))) / (1 - 0.999) > 3
    for: 10m
- Incident template tags: safe_mode_stage, affected_routes, model_variants_switched, evidence_ids
- Automation hook examples:
  - When SLOBurnHigh fires, the alertmanager webhook should: create incident, snapshot dashboards, and optionally (configurable) enact Stage 1 traffic-shaper policy.

Post-Incident Analysis Required Fields (to be present in postmortem):
- What went wrong (concise)
- Why it went wrong (root causal chain)
- Why mitigations worked/didn’t work
- Quantified impact and customer list
- Action items (owner + due date) including: telemetry fixes, capacity adjustments, follow-up experiments (e.g., model footprint reduction), and runbook improvements
- Confidence level in remediation (low/medium/high)
